analysis.title: After the tech bloodbath: buy the dip or brace for more (The great tech reset)
key_insights: Deutsche Bank (Binky Chadha) tactically downgraded tech from overweight to neutral on October 9. Mega-cap growth and tech have since fallen 7% while the rest of the S&P 500 gained 5%, a 12 percentage point relative move in two weeks.
DB estimates tech has roughly 5% more relative downside before reaching the bottom of its long-term trend channel, which has provided support on several earlier occasions.
DB estimates mega-cap growth and tech positioning fell from the 85th percentile in early October to the 33rd percentile, the lowest in six months and close to the lows of the Iran-war selloff.
NDX remains in the range it has held since May. 29k in futures is the make-or-break level, with the 200-day moving average just below at about 28,500.
GS Momentum basket has recorded 30 daily moves of more than 5% in either direction in 2026, more than any other year in the dataset including 2000, 2009 and 2020, with two months left in the year.
VXN has risen from about 20 in mid-September to near 28 with NDX roughly unchanged, about 40% higher implied volatility at the same index level.
Tech volatility has risen alongside widening CDS spreads, with VXN outperforming VIX.

GS sees similarities between the recent tech unwind and July's selloff: about $20bn of TMT sold over two weeks versus $23bn in July, with near-identical moves in the hardest-hit trades. SPX is down 2.4% versus 3.4% in July, and AI stocks are increasingly moving together while index volatility stays contained.
Buying dips toward the 50-day moving average and trendline support in CIBR (cybersecurity) has remained profitable. Cybersecurity is holding up better than the rest of the AI trade.
BTIG data shows the B to CCC credit spread near 8%, seen only four other times since 1996. On each prior occasion the S&P 500 was at least 11.8% below its 52-week high, versus about 2% below now.

Nomura estimates a further 5% equity decline could trigger about $225 billion of selling from index options, leveraged ETF dealers and vol-control strategies. A 3% decline would generate $134 billion of selling, while a 3% rally would produce only $23 billion of buying.

sector_views.rationale: DB tactically downgraded tech from overweight to neutral on October 9 on unfavorable risk/reward, and sees about 5% more relative downside to the bottom of its trend channel.
The Market Ear says the structural bull case in CIBR remains intact and dips toward the 50-day moving average and trendline support have been profitable.
